EVERYDAY APPLIANCES / PRACTICAL ENERGY GUIDE

How much does a refrigerator cost to run?

Start with the annual kWh on the energy label. An illustrative refrigerator using 500 kWh per year costs $80 per year at $0.16/kWh, or about $6.58 for a 30-day period.

Illustrative figures · USD · Replace the example rate with your own

Start with annual kWh

Look for the annual electricity consumption on the appliance's energy label or manufacturer specification, expressed in kWh/year. Multiply this figure by your electricity rate to estimate the annual usage cost.

500 kWh/year × $0.16/kWh = $80 per year

For a daily average, divide annual energy by 365. Here, 500 ÷ 365 is about 1.37 kWh per day. For 30 days, calculate 500 ÷ 365 × 30 × $0.16 = $6.58, rounded to cents.

The dollar cost printed on a U.S. EnergyGuide label uses its own assumptions. The FTC explains that your bill can differ because your energy price and use differ. Using the label's kWh with your own rate makes the price assumption explicit.

Calculate your label-based cost

Enter annual energy in kWh, not watts. These estimates assume the same daily average across a 365-day year. USD is used below; the price and label figures start with illustrative values.

Energy usage cost only. Fixed charges, taxes, and rate changes are additional.

A 30-day estimate and one-twelfth of the annual cost are different: a year has more than 360 days. For the 500 kWh example, the average calendar-month cost is $80 ÷ 12 = $6.67, while the 30-day cost is $6.58.

Why watts times 24 can mislead

A refrigerator can stay plugged in all day while its compressor, fans, and defrost system operate at different times. Electrical input at one moment does not tell you how much energy it consumes across an entire day.

For example, multiplying a 100 W power reading by 24 hours gives 2.4 kWh. That is the energy for a continuous 100 W draw over the full day; it is not automatically the refrigerator's daily consumption.

Use annual label energy for an initial estimate, or measure energy over a representative period. If using the main watts-and-hours calculator, enter measured average power for the period, or a supported estimate of equivalent running hours.

Compare the label with actual use

A label-based estimate is a comparison starting point. Your refrigerator's size, operating environment, settings, and usage may differ from the conditions behind its label.

If a suitable meter records 7 kWh over seven representative days, the measured daily average is 1 kWh. At $0.16/kWh, that is $0.16 per day, or $4.80 over 30 similar days. A longer measurement period can better capture changing operation.

Maintain the appliance according to its manual and follow its storage and operating instructions. Evaluate consumption using your actual measurements rather than assuming that shortening essential refrigeration time is an appropriate way to save energy.
